Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Animals: Dogs, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Vignette:
Lakshmi is a 61-year-old woman who works alongside her husband on a small vegetable farm in California’s Central Valley, a life she has known for over thirty years. Seven months ago, after a long day of picking tomatoes, she was walking back to the storage shed when a man stepped out from behind the irrigation tank. He grabbed her by the wrist, pulled her into the tall weeds near the ditch, and raped her. She remembers the weight of his body, the smell of sweat and diesel, and the sound of a dog barking somewhere close by—a stray that had been roaming the property for weeks. She did not scream; she froze, certain that if she made a sound he would hurt her worse. Afterwards, she lay in the dirt until his footsteps faded, then walked home in a daze, washed herself in the outdoor tap, and told no one.

In the weeks that followed, Lakshmi found she could no longer fall asleep the way she used to. As soon as the lights went out, her body would stiffen, her ears would strain for footsteps or a creaking door, and she would lie awake for hours, convinced that if she let herself drift off she would not hear danger coming. Her husband, Hari, began to notice that she flinched violently when he touched her shoulder from behind, even when he only meant to let her know dinner was ready. She would gasp and pull away, her heart pounding, before her mind had even registered that it was him. She had come to believe that her body was broken in some way—that it could no longer tell the difference between a kind hand and an attack.

The most frightening moments arrived without any warning. She might be walking along the irrigation ditch, focusing on the plants, when a movement in her peripheral vision—a stray dog trotting through the field—would send the entire memory crashing back. Suddenly she was back in the weeds, feeling the dirt against her back, hearing that barking, and the present moment dissolved. It was like a film that played over and over, and she could not stop it. When it happened, she felt as though she were being raped all over again, here and now, not months ago. She could taste the dust, feel the pressure of his hand on her neck. Her body would react before her mind caught up—her muscles would lock, her breathing would turn shallow, and she would freeze on the spot, unable to move or speak for several minutes.

Lakshmi began to avoid the side of the farm where the stray dog had been seen, even though it meant taking a longer route and leaving certain rows of tomatoes unpicked. She started coming inside earlier than usual, before dusk, so she would not have to walk in the half-light. She also began to avoid any time alone with Hari in the bedroom. When he reached for her at night, she would turn away, claiming exhaustion. Intimacy had become a trigger in itself: the feeling of a body moving close to hers, the weight of a hand on her hip, all of it felt like the assault happening again. She never told him why. She was certain he would blame her, or that he would be disgusted that she could not simply get over it.

The consequences accumulated quietly. Hari grew confused and hurt; he began to sleep on the couch, assuming she was angry with him. Work on the farm slowed because Lakshmi avoided large sections of the property, and she stopped volunteering for the weekend market, fearful of the crowds and of being accidentally jostled. She spent more and more time sitting rigidly in the kitchen, waiting for the next sudden memory to strike. Each time a dog barked from a neighboring property, her throat would close and the film would start again.

What finally brought Lakshmi to a clinic was a morning when a customer’s dog barked from the back of a truck at the market—she had decided to go just once more—and she found herself on the ground, shaking, unable to breathe, while strangers stared. The paramedic who helped her up asked if she had been hurt. She said nothing, but later that day she told Hari a fraction of the truth: that something bad had happened in the field, and she could not make the pictures stop. He drove her to a community health center the next morning. Lakshmi does not know if talking can really help. She is mostly afraid that she will spend the rest of her life flinching at every touch and watching that film play behind her eyes. But she is also hoping—just barely—that a person who listens might show her how to turn it off.
